questions.stem: Which structures make up the central nervous system?

options.text: The brain and the spinal cord
options.explanation: Those two structures form the CNS.

options.text: All the nerves of the body
options.explanation: That describes the peripheral nervous system.
Sense organs feed the CNS; they are not it.

options.text: The heart and major blood vessels
options.explanation: That is the circulatory system, a different topic.

options.text: A single neurone stretching the body's length
options.explanation: One neurone is one cell; nerves contain many.
A nerve is defined as a bundle of neurones.

options.text: A muscle that moves the spine
options.explanation: Nerves carry signals, they are not contractile tissue.
Neurotransmitters are the chemicals; nerves are structures.

questions.stem: How does information travel through the nervous system?

options.text: As food molecules absorbed by cells
options.explanation: Nutrition has no signalling role here.

options.text: As sound waves through the bones
options.explanation: Sound only matters inside the ear as a stimulus.
Fast-moving electrical signals pass along neurones.

options.text: As hormones diffusing through the blood
options.explanation: That is hormonal communication, the slower parallel system.

questions.stem: Which role does the central nervous system play in a response?

options.text: It stores energy for the response
options.explanation: Energy storage belongs to liver and adipose tissue.

options.text: It detects the stimulus at the body surface
options.explanation: Receptors in sense organs do the detecting.

options.text: It contracts to move the limbs
options.explanation: Muscles move limbs; the CNS instructs them.

options.text: It processes incoming information and coordinates the body's response
options.explanation: The CNS is the central coordinating centre.

questions.stem: Why do nerves reach the sense organs?

options.text: So receptors there can send impulses into the CNS and receive instructions back
options.explanation: The link carries impulses both into and out of the centre.

options.text: To supply the eyes with oxygen
options.explanation: Blood vessels, not nerves, supply oxygen.
Glands lubricate; nerves signal.

options.text: To anchor the organs in place
options.explanation: Connective tissue anchors; nerves connect.

questions.stem: State the two components of the central nervous system.
questions.modelAnswer: The brain and the spinal cord.

questions.stem: Name the cells that carry electrical impulses, and the bundles they form.
questions.modelAnswer: Neurones carry the impulses, and bundled together they form nerves.

questions.stem: Explain why electrical signalling suits the rapid responses the specification describes.
questions.modelAnswer: Electrical impulses travel along neurones at high speed, so a stimulated receptor can alert the CNS and trigger an effector within a fraction of a second — far faster than chemical transport through blood, which is why nervous responses are described as rapid.

questions.stem: A student's fingertip touches something sharp. List, in order, the structures the signal passes through between the skin and the muscle that pulls away.
questions.modelAnswer: Receptors in the skin fire sensory impulses along sensory neurones into the CNS, which processes them and sends motor impulses along motor neurones to the effector muscles that withdraw the finger.

questions.stem: What do receptors produce when a sense organ is stimulated?

options.explanation: Receptors consume, not produce, oxygen.
Stimulation makes receptors generate electrical impulses.
Glands release hormones; receptors fire impulses.
No cells are created during detection.

questions.stem: Which neurones carry impulses into the CNS?

options.explanation: Relay neurones work inside the CNS, not from the sense organs.
Effectors are muscles and glands, not neurones.
Sensory neurones are the inbound line to the CNS.
Motor neurones carry instructions outward.

questions.stem: Which list of stimulus types matches the sense organs named in this note?

options.explanation: Not part of the IGCSE sense-organ list.
The list is wider than the two obvious senses.
Taste and smell are chemicals, but the other stimuli count too.
These are the detected stimulus classes.

questions.stem: What do effectors do once instructed by motor neurones?

options.explanation: Those are the two effector actions named.
The actions are matched to the wrong tissue types.
Effectors act; they do not build detector cells.

options.text: They send impulses back to the sense organ
options.explanation: Effectors are the endpoint, not another relay.

questions.stem: Why is the receptor-to-effector loop described as automatic and rapid?

options.explanation: Impulses originate at receptors, not effectors.

options.text: Because the impulses travel electrically along neurones without conscious routing
options.explanation: Electrical speed plus fixed pathways gives rapid automatic responses.

options.text: Because each step waits for a hormone to arrive
options.explanation: Hormonal transport is the slower system.

options.text: Because the CNS asks the brain to decide consciously each time
options.explanation: Conscious decision would make it slow and voluntary.

questions.stem: State the direction sensory neurones and motor neurones each carry impulses.
questions.modelAnswer: Sensory neurones carry impulses into the CNS; motor neurones carry them out to effectors.

questions.stem: Name the two effector actions produced at the end of the pathway.
Explain why impulses travel in both directions — inward and outward — during a nervous response.
questions.modelAnswer: The CNS cannot act on a stimulus it has not received, so sensory neurones bring impulses in from the receptors; once it has processed that information it must instruct effectors, so motor neurones carry impulses back out — the two directions are the input and output halves of one loop.

questions.stem: A bright torch flashes into someone's eyes and their pupils narrow. Identify the receptor, the processing centre and the effector in this response.
questions.modelAnswer: Light receptors in the retina are stimulated, the CNS processes the incoming impulses, and circular muscles in the iris are the effectors whose contraction narrows the pupils.
